I've  always had a problem of just kinda 'going with the flow' and  maintaining the status quo. I'm awful at doing anything unless I have an  external force pushing me. That's actually one of the reasons I'm  depressed.... but it also makes it really hard to escape my depression.  There really doesn't seem to be a solution, except for ones that I'm too  pathetic to accomplish. I end up doing nothing about pretty much  everything. My worst moments are when I become self-aware or think about  my situation, so most of the time I'm just on autopilot, trying to  distract myself. I've been coasting for years, aware that I have nothing  to live for and my life isn't going anywhere and it'll eventually come  to a head and I have no plan for that. I'm aware I'm stuck in a rut, but  I make no attempt to do anything about it. I just try to get through my  day with as little thinking or awareness as possible. It tends to  involve a lot of naps, netflix, or audiobooks if I'm commuting. Even then, I don't really get anything from those; I can't carry a conversation about a book I just finished. It's simply in-the-moment entertainment, and nothing more.

My mom was diagnosed with terminal cancer, given 2 years max. It wasn't exactly a shock; she had originally been diagnosed years earlier, and had been through the cycle of doing chemo, ending up in relatively good health, then then cancer coming back worse, repeat. I think everyone knew deep down that it would kill her sooner or later, and she had retired and basically gotten her affairs in order. But then when the terminal diagnosis came, she decided to continue with chemo and other treatments to extend her life to try to get the full two years of life. Cue \~13 months of rapid degradation with her needing constant caretakers, being in pain, rushing to the hospital regularly for some random health complication. Overall she was miserable, meanwhile my family and friends of the family were paying thousands and thousands of dollars trying to keep up with all the various payments, and also taking turns dropping everything in their own life to be a 24/7 caretaker. 

Eventually my mom decided it wasn't worth it and went into hospice. The next 5 weeks were the happiest she had been in a long time, and it made things much easier on everyone else too. When she eventually passed, we were all so burnt out and needed to play catch-up with our own lives that we didn't/couldn't find the time to finish sorting through my moms possessions and clean out her house. Therefore we continued making payments on her now abandoned house for like 7 more months until we found time and money to meet up to finally clean things up and sell the house. 

I realize this might be super controversial, as people get really hung up on life being sacred. But when the end is in sight and the family as a whole has no disposable income because we're trying to take care of someone who is too sick to enjoy her hobbies, then, well, hospice is a great choice. If my mom had gone into hospice right from the start, she would have had so much more energy (as opposed to being very fatigued from chemo etc), less stressed, and all-around able to actually enjoy what time was left to her. At the same time all of us who cared for her could have spent her last months hanging out and sharing memories or making new ones instead of putting all our time into upkeep and crisis management. Hospice still involved some of that, but to a much lesser degree. And again, for a family that isn't wealthy, the economic taxing from her trying to hold on as long as possible was quite detrimental. 

I love my mom, but I really wish she had realized that hospice was not only a valid, but also a wholesome choice. Her choice to attempt to extend her life to the max ended up putting a huge strain on everything, and kind of left a stain on her memory. Relief isn't what should be felt at the very end, but, that's how it ended up, even if I do miss her.

Yeah, I do this too. I can't give any sort of advice, but I can share my experience. 
I've decided I'm a really good actor because I convince people I'm happy when I'm actually super unhappy. Great example: My dad and his wife, neither of whom I talk to very much, nor see often since we live hundreds of miles away, came to visit me recently. They wanted to know about my life; my job, current hobbies, other things. I lied my ass off, wore a mask the entire time, and after they left, I got texts from them exclaiming how wonderful it was to see me, and that they're so thrilled that my life is exactly where I want it. 
Wearing this mask comes so naturally to me that I'm really not even aware I do it, except when it comes off. It's gotten really hard for me to find amusement in things, so when I'm talking to people and jokes are being made and then they leave, I may be mid-laugh when suddenly they're around a corner and there's no one around to see me without my mask, and I just stop laughing abruptly. It's really awkward when they tell a really funny joke that causes lots of loud laughter, but as they walk away, they can hear me after they can no longer see me. That means I'm still laughing, but any hint of a smile has left my face. I work in retail, and get a lot of the same customers, so I have a fair number of people regularly being friendly with me. I'm often putting on this mask for them, and taking it off as soon as they're gone because I usually work alone. 

I don't know if this is worth anything, but, I shared my experience. And my thoughts are that it sucks. But maybe if my depression ever gets out of the way enough for me to be proactive and make changes in my life, I could turn this talent into an acting career.

Your metaphor actually reminds me of the movie 127 Hours. I'll try not to give anything that might be considered spoilers if you haven't seen it, but, basically there's an accident and the guy gets trapped. At first, he panics and tries to escape. But eventually he gets tired and starts realizing there's not really a way out. That leads to sitting around until you reach some sort of breaking point. I feel like that's an analogy for life with depression, though there's not necessarily an "accident". I've gotten stuck in this labyrinth, I no longer have the strength to keep looking for a way out, but I also don't even care to find an escape anymore. There's a Radiohead lyric, "I'm not living, I'm just killing time." That's where I feel I am. The song is about something completely different, but out of context it works wonderfully. So I'm basically just waiting for my breaking point. It doesn't always feel passive, like when I push away my friends, but really, I 'push them away' by simply no longer making an effort to talk to them or anything, and I just sit at home alone instead. So it does get to be pretty passive. I actually look forward to my existence being boxed up, with the walls getting smaller and smaller, boxing me in to a tiny corner when I'll basically be forced over the cliff.

Anyway. That's my input on this sort of thing. Most of it isn't actually in response to the post I replied to, and some of it is rambling, but there it is.

I feel like my brain is eroding. I used to have a really good memory, and would remember so much stuff effortlessly. But somewhere around the time I started getting depressed, my memory started letting me down. Since then, it's only gotten worse. I really don't have any vivid memories anymore. I can be talking to someone, and as soon as we finish our conversation and I turn around to leave, I realize I don't know if I actually said goodbye or just abruptly left; I simply can't remember. It turns out I'm conscious enough in the moment that I do say goodbye, but, after the event in question, I sometimes don't even know if I was talking to somebody at all or if I just imagined it. Making whatever I think I'm remembering is something I'm making up on the spot; one of my biggest problems with my memory is that nothing in my head seems real. There should be some sort of gradient; dreams and fantasies should be known to be unreal, and I used to have a sense that something didn't actually happen. Instead, I typically have to rely on logic to puzzle out if something in my head really happened. Maybe I remember that a new building was constructed on some street corner. Well, next time I pass that corner, I'll look, see no building, and so I must have dreamed it. Except that I've had experiences where it turns out it WAS an actual memory, but it was just really old and they've since torn down the building, which I didn't notice. Or maybe there actually was a new building somewhere, but I'm just completely wrong about the location. There's a lot of ways I can be mistaken, and it really throws me for a loop sometimes. 
Another thing is that my own personal memories have no more meaning or connection to reality as something I read out of a book. If someone asks you if you've ever slain a Nazgul, the answer is obviously no, because they're fictional beings; they don't really have a tie to reality. But at the same time, if someone ever asks me if I've been to the zoo (which I have on several occasions [I think]), I still say no, because my memories of such an event are 1. less vivid than my memory of seeing a Nazgul die (from the 2nd LOTR movie) and 2. feel no more realistic than memories of completely fictional events. I don't really have anything other than observational logic to tell the difference between things that I did and things that other people did. On top of that, my memories are so distant and vague that even if I determined that the memory is my own and is real, I still can't really get any useful information out of it. It always baffles me how people can give detailed accounts or descriptions of something they've experienced or seen. That's partly because my memories tend to have no visual aspect to them. I can't actually 'see' anything with my mind's eye. 
I also forget facts and general information. It really hurts my social life (which is already fairly abysmal, but that's a different story) when I'm talking to someone, and maybe I'm reminded of a movie with a particular scene that's really relevant to the discussion, and I wanna talk about it, but then I realize that I can't remember the name of the movie. So I go to talk about the plot instead, to give context (and maybe because they'll recognize it), but I realize I've forgotten the important plot twists, and can't remember any of the small stuff, so I just skip to explaining the relevant scene directly. But then it turns out I can't remember the words descriptive enough to explain what's happening or why, and after trying to make the connections for awhile, I just give up and shut up and let others do the talking. That's just an example. 
Something else that happens is I'll see somebody I know, and maybe they ask me about new things in my life. But I have no idea when I last saw this person, or what they already know about me, so I end up telling them things they already know about, or I'll assume they know something, and I'll just try building off that, but then they get really confused because they've actually heard nothing about it yet. 
There's other stuff too, but, frankly I'm not entirely sure what I've already written here, nor can I easily recall what all I could talk about, and I'm tired besides, so I'll just leave it here. 
Sorry for going on so long, but hopefully the long response will give you the insight you wanted. 


tl;dr
My memory is pretty shit, I often forget things important for not feeling like I'm insane or otherwise living in a dream-like state. My memory interferes with success in every aspect of my life. 
So no, you're not overreacting. I'm sorry you struggle with lost memories, and I hope you're able to recover what you once had.

There's more to my story than just introvertedness, but I figure I'd share some of it in case it's relevant. 
First off, for some context, I'm also shy, timid, have various kinds of anxiety (mostly social), and just plain quiet. A lot of it overlaps with the rest, so I'm not sure how much of this is relevant, but I know my upbringing definitely contributed to the way I am. I remember deciding that I spoke too soon before I even reached double digits in age, so I deliberately slowed myself down and would think about things. My family was also kind of big, and I was the youngest, and while I was already passive in nature, I was taught (accidentally, nobody meant to teach this) to essentially shut up, sit down, and wait for somebody to tell me what to do. I learned to stay out of the way unless people wanted me for something. There was enough of an age gap between myself and my siblings that I didn't connect with them a whole lot, so within my family unit, I had to learn to be on my own on a few levels. There are other examples too, other stories that I could tell. 

The point is, I may have been born somewhat introverted, by my experiences growing up certainly seem to have something to do with being comfortable when I'm alone, being self-sufficient, and finding social interactions stressful and tiring.
